walkthroughs.body_html:
Theme 3: Business Behaviour and the Labour Market — a core area of A-Level Economics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Theme 3: Business Behaviour and the Labour Market brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Theme 3: Business Behaviour and the Labour Market.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: In perfect competition long-run equilibrium, firms earn:
options: Supernormal profit
Normal profit
Losses
Monopoly rent
P > MC
P = MC
P < MC
P = AC

mcqs.q: What does standard theory predict about a minimum wage?
options: If above equilibrium, it raises wages for those still employed but causes unemployment by reducing labour demand — though empirical evidence is mixed.
A negative externality is a tax on a business.
A minimum wage always reduces unemployment because workers have more money to spend.
A minimum wage is paid by the government.
A negative externality is something bad that happens to a business.
A negative externality is a tax on a business.
A cost imposed on a third party not involved in the transaction — e.g. pollution from a factory affects neighbours who didn't choose to bear it.
Demand always falls when supply increases.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between a shift in demand and a movement along the demand curve?
options: A movement along the curve is caused by a change in price; a shift of the whole curve is caused by changes in other factors (income, tastes, substitute prices).
Demand always falls when supply increases.
A change in price shifts the demand curve.
A minimum wage is paid by the government.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Perfect competition”?
options: Price below average variable cost; firm closes in the short run to limit losses to fixed costs.
Producing at the lowest point on average cost curve; firms in perfect competition long-run achieve this.
Profit above normal; in perfect competition only in the short run; entry erodes it.
Many firms, homogeneous product, perfect information, free entry/exit; firms are price takers.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Allocative efficiency”?
options: Price equals marginal cost (P = MC); consumer welfare maximised; achieved in perfect competition long-run.
Producing at the lowest point on average cost curve; firms in perfect competition long-run achieve this.
Price below average variable cost; firm closes in the short run to limit losses to fixed costs.
Just enough revenue to cover all costs including opportunity cost of capital; long-run equilibrium in perfect competition.
